post.description: Platform staff only. The target must have enabled support access or be covered by an active grant — the service refuses otherwise, and this endpoint cannot override that. Returns an access token whose subject is the target user and whose actor is the caller; every action taken with it is attributed to both.

Called BY the impersonated session, which is the only caller that holds the JTI being revoked. It takes no parameters for that reason: everything it needs — which session, which target, which actor — comes from the token, so it cannot be pointed at somebody else's session.

Redeems an enrolment token and returns this host's agent-scoped key and secret. The host is admitted into an ORGANIZATION, not a fleet — joining one is a task, so a new host and a host migrating between fleets follow the same path. Idempotent on machine_id: a rebuilt hypervisor re-enrols onto the same MACHINE record with a fresh credential rather than leaving a permanently-offline ghost. A machine a capacity sync has already discovered in a cluster is adopted rather than duplicated, matched by the node name its hostname implies.

post.description: One request carries both, deliberately: two endpoints would give a bee two ways to be 'seen', and a bee parked on a long poll would have to heartbeat separately to avoid looking dead. Declare unavailable_for_seconds BEFORE doing anything that interrupts the host — a reboot is indistinguishable from a failure unless the host says in advance that it is coming back.

So a fleet operation can be watched without SSH-ing to a hypervisor mid-rotation, which during an evacuation is often the one thing you must not do. Lines carry a per-task sequence assigned by the bee; resending a batch is a no-op.

post.description: Terminal reports are idempotent. A bee that finishes and dies before its report is acknowledged will report again on restart, and rejecting the duplicate would strand the task against a host that considers it done.

Returns the plaintext credential ONCE. Only its hash is stored, so a key that is not captured from this response is replaced rather than recovered — no endpoint reissues or reveals one.

A user-scoped key needs nothing beyond membership: it acts as you and can do nothing you cannot. An org-scoped key is standing access to the whole tenant, so it requires admin and refuses impersonated sessions — an operator acting as a user must not be able to leave themselves a way back in. Agent-scoped keys are refused outright; they are issued only by fleet enrolment.

delete.description: Revocation is permanent and takes effect on the next request the key makes. You may revoke your own user-scoped keys. Revoking one of the organization's org-scoped keys requires admin and refuses impersonated sessions, for the same reason minting one does: it changes the tenant's standing access, and that has to be attributable to a real admin. Nobody may revoke another person's user key.

delete.description:
Revokes this agent's credential and then deletes its record. The MACHINE survives as agentless — its cluster membership, address and onboarding history are on the hypervisor record, not on the agent — so this is 'remove the agent', never 'forget the box'.

The credential is revoked FIRST and the revocation is verified before anything is deleted. It lives in the control database while the agent record lives in the tenant database, so no transaction covers both: deleting first and failing to revoke would leave a live agent key with nothing pointing at it, and nothing lists agent-scoped keys.

Refused with 409 while an onboarding worker holds a lease on this machine — it is installing and enrolling right now, and would either race the delete or resurrect the record behind it.

The agent process on the host is NOT stopped. It keeps running and starts failing authentication, which is the intended outcome: the credential is what this revokes.

post.description:
Admits a host into the ORGANIZATION, not into a cluster. Joining one is a task, so a brand-new host starts in the same fleetless state a migrating host passes through — which means an agent can be provisioned before any cluster exists.

Impersonated sessions are refused: an operator acting as somebody else must not be able to mint something that admits a machine to the fleet.

get.description:
Machines with no hive: onboarded but not yet joined to a cluster, or departed from one. Every migration passes through this state and a failed arrival leaves a machine sitting in it.

Each entry carries its onboarding state, because a machine that has not finished onboarding has no agent and an arrival pointed at it will fail at the SSH.
get.summary: List machines belonging to no hive

post.description: Queues the arrival. Refused with 409 and reason codes when the host already belongs to a hive, still carries guests, or the target has no nodes to join to.
post.summary: Add a standalone machine to a hive

get.description: Every hive in the caller's organization, with the node count and whether a capacity sync can run for it. A hive with no API URL or credential is never synced, so every node in it reads as never-observed and every departure refuses.

delete.description:
Refuses while the cluster still holds hypervisors. A hypervisor row is the durable record of a physical machine — its machine id, its onboarding history, the agent bound to it — so deleting the cluster out from under one would either destroy that or leave it pointing at a cluster that no longer exists.

Depart the nodes first; each one becomes fleetless and keeps its identity, and the cluster can then be removed.

patch.description: Only the fields present are changed. Setting an API URL and a credential is what makes a hive syncable.

post.description:
The same job the schedule runs, enqueued immediately. Most often wanted after a departure refused with drain_unknown, which means the last observation is too stale to say whether a node is empty.

The job is unique per hive while queued or running, so asking twice gets the sync already on its way rather than a second one.
post.summary: Refresh a hive's capacity observations now

get.description:
Every MACHINE this organization owns, in a cluster or not. Each carries three independent statuses — provisioning_state (has the agent been installed), schedulable plus drain_state (may new work land here), and bee_status (is it answering right now) — because a machine can be provisioned AND cordoned AND offline at the same instant, and one badge cannot say that.

When a node cannot leave its hive, the reasons why are computed by the same gate the departure job runs, so a client never has to reimplement it. A machine in no hive reports not_a_member and appears in /fleet/fleetless as well.
get.summary: List machines with their three status axes

post.description: Cordoning withdraws the node from NEW placements. It does not evict anything: draining is a separate act, and conflating them would mean the only way to stop new work was to move existing work. A cordon is the first step of every departure.

Queues the departure. The host is left standalone and belonging to no fleet; it does NOT join anything. A migration is a departure and then an arrival, and the fleetless state between them is real rather than a window to hurry through.

Refused with 409 and a list of reason codes when the host is not drained, the hive is too small, or the capacity observation is too stale to decide. The same gate runs again inside the job, against state read in one transaction.
post.summary: Remove a hypervisor from its hive

post.description:
Sets provisioning_state back to `pending` and clears the attempt count. This RECORDS INTENT; it does not queue a job. Onboarding is self-scheduling — a ticker claims pending rows under a lease — so there is nothing to enqueue and nothing that has to be running for the request to be meaningful.

Allowed from `failed` and from `provisioned` — the latter is 'revive', and it is safe because onboarding skips enrolment for a host that is already heartbeating, so a re-run does not invalidate a working agent's credential.

Refused with 409 while a lease is live: redriving a row a worker holds puts two workers on one host, both installing keys and reloading sshd. An EXPIRED lease is redrivable — that is the recovery path for a worker killed mid-onboard.

provisioning_error is deliberately NOT cleared. An operator watching a machine retry wants to see what it is retrying past, and it is overwritten by the next real failure.

Refused with 409 while that bee already has an outstanding task. At most one at a time is what makes 'what is this hypervisor doing' answerable from a single row.

fleet.datacenter.evict is issued to a node that will REMAIN, naming the one to remove — a node cannot remove itself from a cluster it is leaving.

post.description: Requires admin. Impersonated sessions are refused: an operator acting as a user must not be able to invite an account they control. The organization comes from the session, never from the request.

Issues NO session. A new invitee chooses a password here and then signs in through /auth/login; an existing account gains the membership and signs in as it already could. Keeping session minting on the login path alone means lockout, MFA and the email-confirmation gate cannot be skipped by arriving through this door.

get.description: Lets the accept page render before the invitee commits to anything: which organization, which address, and whether they need to choose a password or sign in. Holding the token is the authorization — it was mailed to the address it names.

delete.description: The organization is taken from the session and used as a query predicate, so an id belonging to another tenant answers 404 rather than revoking anything.

Refused while this account is the only owner of an organization — see /me/sole-ownerships. Every session is revoked and every authentication factor removed. The record itself is retained: audit events, fleet tasks and invitations name the actor, and an audit trail that vanishes with the account is one the audited person can erase.

get.description: Returns the authenticated user's profile, MFA status, and organization.

patch.description: Update the authenticated user's first name, last name, or email.

get.description: Returns the organizations the authenticated user belongs to.

put.description: Change the authenticated user's password. Requires the current password.

get.description: Deleting an account is refused while it is the only owner of an organization, because that would leave a tenant nobody can administer. This names them, so the answer is actionable rather than just a refusal.
Any member may see who else is in their organization. Roles are included because they determine who to ask for access.
get.summary: List the members of this organization

delete.description: Requires admin, and an owner to remove an owner. The last owner cannot be removed.
delete.summary: Remove a member from this organization

patch.description: Requires admin, and an owner for anything crossing the owner line in either direction. The last owner cannot be demoted. Impersonated sessions are refused: an operator acting as a user must not be able to grant themselves standing access.

parameters.description: The membership id, not the user id.

get.description: Each kind shows this organization's own position AND the effective result, because 'what applies to us' is the question being asked and neither level answers it alone. A restriction merges toward strictness: the platform's floor cannot be lowered here, only raised.

put.description: Requires admin. Impersonated sessions are refused: an operator acting as a user must not be able to change that organization's security posture under their name. Note that disabling here does NOT switch off a platform policy — a restriction merges toward strictness, so an organization can raise the floor but never lower it.
put.summary: Set a policy for this organization

get.description: Scoped to this organization. Ask before enabling — the alternative is finding out from the people who can no longer sign in.
get.summary: How many members this policy would lock out

delete.description: OWNER only, and impersonated sessions are refused. The organization stops resolving immediately: its tenant database becomes unreachable, every session scoped to it is revoked, and its agents can no longer authenticate. Key material is NOT destroyed by this call — the organization row holds the only key that can decrypt the tenant database, so erasing it would destroy the data irreversibly rather than merely retiring it. Purging is a separate operator step, which is what leaves a way back.

get.description: Every rule that gates authentication, organization creation and invitation acceptance, across every tenant. Rows written by the boot-time public-domain seed are marked, as are the ones an operator has overridden to allow — that divergence exists only in this table and nothing else reports it.

post.description: Purpose is required and has no default. Email rules beat domain rules, and among domain rules the most specific wins; anything that is not exactly 'allow' denies.

delete.description: Answers with a body rather than 204 because deleting a SEEDED rule does not last: the next boot re-creates it as a create_org deny. The response says so explicitly. Re-creating is fail-safe and stays that way — being silent about it was the problem.

put.description: Policy and reason only. Kind, value and purpose are the rule's identity — retargeting one is a delete and a create, so that both facts stay visible. This is also the durable way to permit a seeded public domain: an update survives every restart, whereas a delete is undone by the next one.

get.description: Every policy kind, whether or not the platform has an opinion on it. A kind the platform has never set reads as 'inherit', which is the identity element of the merge.

delete.description: Deleting is how the platform withdraws its opinion. That is NOT the same as disabling: a disabled policy contributes nothing to the merge either, but it is a stated position, and the distinction is what an organization sees when deciding whether it needs its own.
delete.summary: Return a platform policy to inherit

put.description: Impersonated sessions are refused: a platform policy applies to every tenant, and an operator acting as somebody else should not be able to change it under their name.

get.description: Ask BEFORE enabling. Turning on require_mfa across a platform where half the users have never enrolled a factor locks them out at their next request, and the only signal is a support queue.
get.summary: How many users this policy would lock out

get.description: Public halves and fingerprints. The private half is never returned by any endpoint — it is unsealed only inside a River worker, so a fleet-wide credential never passes through a response, a log or an error tracker.

post.description: Creates an Ed25519 keypair. The private half is sealed with this organization's own key and never leaves the control plane; the public half is returned in authorized_keys form for whitelisting on hypervisors. Requires admin and refuses impersonated sessions: this key opens root on every host that trusts it, and an operator acting as a customer must not be able to mint one they could later use.

delete.description: Marks the key unusable. It does NOT remove the public half from any hypervisor — that happens when the agents next converge, so a revoked key stays whitelisted on a host that is offline. The row is kept rather than deleted, so a fingerprint found in an authorized_keys file later can still be attributed to something.
